Original article content preserved below:

이번 포스팅에서는 저번 시간에 계속적으로 배웠던 '가우스 소거법(Gauss Elimination)' (줄여서 'GE'라고 부르기도 한다.)에서 이끌어낼 수 있는
LU 분할
에 대해서 알아보려고 한다. 기본적으로 가우스 소거법의 계산과정을 알아야 LU분할이라는 개념이 이해가 되기 때문에 가우스 소거법을 모른다면 이전 포스팅을 참고하자.
(가우스 소거법을 알고 싶다면?
https://techblog-history-younghunjo1.tistory.com/67
)
앞으로 소개할 목차는 다음과 같다.
1. LU Decomposition (LU분할)
2. Triangular Factors
3. Pivoting을 고려한 LU분할
1. LU Decomposition
사람에 따라 LU Factorization이라고도 부르기도 한다. LU분할 개념에 대해서 말로 설명할 수 없는 부분이라고 생각해서 이전에 가우스 소거법 포스팅에서 들었던 똑같은 3개 미지수(변수)에 대한 연립방정식의 예시를 들면서 살펴보자.
LU 분할을 알아보자.
먼저 왼쪽 위의
RAW
라고 된 부분 처럼 3개의 연립방정식이 존재한다. 각 식을 1,2,3번의 식이라고 정의해두고 이전에 배웠던 가우스 소거법을 통해
[ 2번식 - (1번식*2) ]
를 해주어 미지수 u에 대한 계수를 0으로 만들어 주었다. 우리는 이를 행렬을 통해서 표현할 수 있다. 즉, 어떤 행렬(E21 이라고 적혀있는 행렬)를 주어진 행렬(RAW를 A행렬이라고 하자.)
A에다가 곱했을 때 나오는 값이 가우스 소거법을 통해서 나오게 되는 행렬과 똑같아 진다.
이 때 우리는 어떤 행렬(E21)을 구하게 된다. 그리고
E21이라고 표현한 이유는 1번식을 이용해 2번식을 계산하는 행렬
이기 때문이다. 똑같은 과정을 거쳐 1번식을 이용해 3번식을 계산하는 E31 행렬을 구해준다.
그리고 미지수 v를 소거해주기 위해서 2번식을 이용해 3번식을 계산하는 E32행렬에 방금 전에 구했던
'E31*E21*A'
행렬을 곱해주어 구해주게 된다. 그러면 우리가 본질적으로 구하려고 했던
U(U
pper
triangular Matrix)
가 나오게 되며 미지수의 값들을 구할 수 있게 된다.
또 하나 우리가 눈여겨보야할 점은 우리가 그동안 구했던 E라는 행렬에 대한 것이다.
E는 Elementary Matrix의 E
를 의미한다.(고등학교 시절 배웠던 항등원 행렬 E는 선형대수에서는 I라고 나타낸다. 이전 포스팅에서도 언급했다.) 밑의 그림을 보자.
LU 분할이란!?
우리가 구했던 E32, E31, E21을 일반화시키게 되면
노란색으로 칠해진 요소가 속해있는 행렬
처럼 나타낼 수 있다. 또한 모든 E 행렬(Elementary Matirx)의 역행렬을 구할 수 있다. 예를들어 이전에 수행했던 가우스 소거법 계산과정에서 2번식을 계산하기 위해 1번식에 특정 실수값을 곱했을 때의
그 실수값의 부호만 바꾸어서 취해주면 되는 것
이다.(초록색으로 칠해져있는 요소가 들어있는 행렬 참고)
따라서 우리는 위와 같이 E 행렬의 역행렬을 구할 수 있게 됬고 이제 기존에 주어진
A라는 행렬을 여러 E 행렬들의 역행렬들과 U(Upper triangular Matrix)의 곱
으로 나타낼 수 있다. 그리고 여러 E 행렬들의 역행렬들끼리만 연산하게 되면
파란색으로 세모를 그린 부분의 행렬
이 나오게 된다. 우리는 그러한 행렬을 대각 행렬 1을 기준으로 밑에가 0이 아닌 부분이라고 해서
Lower Triangular Matrix
라고 부르게 되며 결국 행렬
A = LU
로 분할을 할 수 있게 된다.
2. Triangular Factors
Traingular Factors는 삼각형 인수라고 할 수 있다. 즉, 여기서는 우리가 앞에서 구했던
LU 행렬의 형태가 Triangular Factors
라고 할 수 있다. 우리는 A라는 연립방정식에서 x라는 미지수(앞의 예시에서 u,v,w 값들)를 곱했을 때 새로운 실수 b가 나온다는 것을 보았다. 이 때 A라는 행렬은 LU분할을 취해줄 수 있다.
그렇다면 이러한 LU 분할은 대체 무슨의미를 갖는걸까? 시스템에서 예시를 들어보자. 밑의 그림과 같이 A라는 시스템이 존재한다. 우리는 A라는 시스템에 미지수 u,v,w를 input으로 넣어주고 b1,b2,b3라는 결과값을 얻게 된다.
b1,b2,b3라는 결과값을 얻게 해주는 것은 바로 u,v,w의 계수가 파라미터 역할을 해주는 것
이다. 그런데 이러한
파라미터의 최적의 값을 찾아주기 위해서는 LU 분할을 이용
하는 것이다.
LU분할을 왜 사용할까?
따라서 우리는
A라는 시스템을 A자체로 설계하는 것이 아닌 LU분할로 나누어 설계하는게 좋다.
그리고
Diagonal Matrix
에 대해서 잠시 알아보자. 기본적으로 정의는 대각행렬이라는 뜻이며 대각행렬은 기본적으로
대각 행렬의 값 빼고 나머지 값들은 모두 0
이다. 밑의 그림을 살펴보자.
Diagonal Matrix(대각행렬)
Upper Martix인 U 행렬이 다음과 같이 주어졌다고 가정하자. 이는 우리가 대각행렬(Diagonal Matrix)를 이용해서 풀어줄 수가 있게 된다. 따라서 U행렬은 D(대각행렬)과 또 하나의 Upper Matrix
(대각행렬이 1인 U와 대각행렬인 d1~dn인 행렬과는 다른 U이다.)
와의 곱으로 나타내줄 수 있고 결국
A = LDU
라는 식이 도출되게 된다.
또한 임의의
행렬 A가 LU분할이 가능하다
는 것은
행렬 A에 대한 LU분할 조합이 2가지 이상이 아닌 unique하다는 것
을 의미한다.
3. Pivoting을 고려한 LU분할
지금까지 우리는 Pivoting을 고려하지 않은 상태로 계산해왔다.
Pivoting이란 미지수를 소거하기 위해서 연립방정식의 순서를 올바르게 바꿔주는 것
을 말한다.
#Pivoting 개념에 대해서 자세하게 알고 싶다면? :
https://techblog-history-younghunjo1.tistory.com/67
Pivoting을 고려한 LU분할
여기서 등장하는 또하나의 개념
Permutation Matrix
라는 'P' 행렬이다.
P 행렬은 항등원 행렬인 'I'행렬과 같은 열들을 가지며 1의 값이 열과 행에 1번씩은 무조건 나오게 된다.
위의 예시 속 P21이라는 것은 2번,1번 연립방정식의 나열 위치를 서로 바꾼 것을 의미한다.
'P'행렬의 중요한 특징은
"P행렬의 역행렬 = P행렬의 Transpose 행렬"
이 같다는 것이다. 따라서 이로 인해 우리는 Pivoting을 고려했을 때
A = P^T*L*U
가 되게 된다.(
단, P행렬의 교환법칙은 성립하지 않는다.
)

Start by deciding whether the goal is explaining `Y` with other variables, modeling time as the main driver, or forecasting a series from its own lagged behavior.
Before choosing a model, inspect the series for non-stationarity, changing variance, changing mean, seasonality, or structural breaks.
If the process grows by a constant amount, a linear trend model is natural. If it grows by a constant rate, a log-linear trend is usually more appropriate.
After fitting a trend model, test residuals for serial correlation. If residuals are still autocorrelated, autoregressive structure is missing and an AR-style model may be needed.
An AR model uses lagged values such as `X_(t-1)` to explain the current value `X_t`. This only makes sense if the process is covariance-stationary: constant mean, finite variance, and time-invariant covariance structure.
If the series has a unit root, it behaves like a random walk and is non-stationary. The Dickey-Fuller family of tests checks that null. First differencing is the standard repair when a unit root is present.
If differencing produces a stationary series, autoregressive modeling becomes more defensible. If seasonality remains, seasonal terms or seasonal differencing must be considered.
ARCH effects mean the variance of the error term changes over time as a function of past errors. Ignoring ARCH can invalidate standard OLS-style inference even when the mean equation looks reasonable.
This note also ties the regression diagnostics back to time series: heteroskedasticity, serial correlation, and model misspecification are not isolated pathologies. They are often the reason a trend or ARIMA-family model fails to produce trustworthy inference or forecasting performance.

Original article content preserved below:

※해당 게시물에 사용된 일부 자료는 순천향대학교 빅데이터공학과 정영섭 교수님의 머신러닝 전공수업 자료에 기반하였음을 알려드립니다.
이번 포스팅에서는 선형대수의 벡터를 기반으로 하는 모델들에 대해서 알아보려고 한다. 앞으로 소개할 모델들을 이해하기 위해서는
벡터공간에서의 기저(Basis)에 대한 개념 이해가 중요
하다. 필자도 이 모델에 대한 수업을 들으면서 선형대수의 기초 개념 공부의 필요성을 느꼈고 개인적으로 오픈 소스 강의를 통해 학습을 진행하고 있다.
앞으로 소개할 목차는 다음과 같다.
1. 기본적으로 알고가야 할 개념
2. Eigen Value(고유값) Decomposition
3. SVD(Singular Value Decomposition)
4. PCA(Principal Component Analysis)
5. LDA(Linear Discriminant Analysis)
1. 기본적으로 알고가야 할 개념
우선적으로 사전적으로 알고있어야 할 몇 가지 개념부터 짚고 넘어가자.
1-1. 기저(Basis)
임의의 벡터공간 V에 대하여
벡터집합 S가 서로 '1차 독립'
이면서 벡터공간 V를 생성하면
벡터집합 S = V의 기저(Basis)
라고 할 수 있다. 이렇게 말로 풀어쓰기만 한다면 무슨 소린지 이해가 잘 안갈 것이다. 다음 그림을 보자.
기저란 무엇일까?
위와 같이 x축 , y축으로 이루어진 벡터공간 V가 있다고 가정하자. 이 때 벡터공간 V의
기저는 바로 x축, y축
2개가 될 수 있다는 것이다.
1-2. 고유벡터(Eigen Vector)와 고유값(Eigen Value)
먼저
고유벡터
란, 어떤 벡터에 선형변환을 취했을 때 방향은 변하지 않고 크기(양=길이)만 변환되는 벡터
를 말한다. 다시 말해, 임의의 정방행렬
A를 특정 벡터(V1)과 곱했을 때, 임의의 실수 람다(
λ)와 특정 벡터(V1)를 곱했을 때 똑같이 나오는 것
을 말한다. 이에 대한 수식은 다음과 같다.
고유벡터란!?
다음 그림을 보자.
고유벡터와 고유값이란 무엇일까?
우리는 기존의 벡터인 x=(2,3)에 변환을 가해주는 연산행렬 A를 취해주었을 때 Ax=(8,7)로 변하게 되는 것이다. 이렇게 변하게 되는 과정에서는 고유벡터와 고유값이 관여한다. 고유벡터에 대한 개념은 위에서 말했던 것과 같은 개념이고
고유값
은 윗 그림의
수식의 실수인 람다(
λ) 값
이 되게 되는 것
이다.
즉, 고유값은 위 그림에서 들은 예시처럼 기존의 벡터 x=(2,3) 을 변환 후 벡터인 Ax=(8,7)로
"얼마나 축소하고 확대를 했는지에 대한 값"
이다.
#참고로 n by n 정방행렬일 때, 고유벡터의 개수는 n개이다.
1-3. 행렬계수(Rank)
행렬계수는 종류를 우선 나누어서 설명하는 것이 이해가 더 쉬울 것 같다.
Column Rank : 선형독립인 열 벡터의 개수
Row Rank : 선형독립인 행 벡터의 개수
#행 벡터와 열 벡터에 대해서 모른다면 밑의 그림을 참고하자.
행 벡터와 열 벡터란?
여기서 만약
모든 행이나 열이 다 '0'이 되게 된다면 서로의 조합으로 생길 수 있다는 것을 의미하고 이는 결국 서로 선형독립이 아님을 방증
하며 행렬계수를 계산하게 될 때는 다
'0'이 되는 행 또는 열을 개수로 포함시키지 않는다.
행렬계수로 세지 않을 때는 모든 행 또는 열 element가 0일 때
2. EigenValue Decomposition
고유값 분해(Decomposition)는 변환 후 벡터가 변환 전 벡터에서
얼마나 확대, 축소를 가했는지를 파악
하기 위함이다.
이제 위에서 배웠던 개념을 적용해보는 시간이다. 다음 필기 그림을 보자.
Eigen Value Decomposition 이란 무엇인가?
고유값 분해는 기본적으로 N by N 정방행렬을 반드시 필요
로 한다. 즉 이
N by N 정방행렬 A에 대해서 3개 행렬(벡터)의 내적으로 나타낼 수 있다는 것
이다. 필기 그림 속에 등장하는 고유값, 고유벡터에 대한 설명을
색
깔
볼펜으로 잘 써놓았으니 읽으면서 이해하면 도움이 된다. 한 가지 추가적으로 말할 것은
파란색
글씨의
'New 축'
이라는 것인데, 이 '새로운 축'이라는 의미는
이전에 사용했던 그림자료에서 V1이라는 고유벡터의 새로운 '관점'에서 바라보는 것
이다.
New 축이라는 것은 고유벡터 v1(또는 v2)를 의미한다.
3. SVD(Singular Value Decomposition)
그렇다면 정방행렬이 아닌
직사각형 행렬(ex. m by n)일 때
는 어떻게 할까? 이 때는
SVD를 사용
한다. Decomposition은 '분할'이라는 뜻으로 이름 그대로,
m by n 행렬에 대해 3개의 행렬 내적으로 나타내는 것
이다. 우선 그림을 보기 전에 SVD의
가장 중요한 포인트
는 직사각 행렬 m by n에 임의의 행렬 A라는 연산을 취했을 때
벡터의 방향만 변하고
양(길이)는 절대 변하지 않음
을 기억하자.
SVD의 Process
SVD의 프로세스에 대해서 알아보자. 우선 위 그림에서 m by n 이라는 A 행렬을 다음과 같은 3개의 행렬의 곱으로 나타낸다.
U 행렬 : A행렬보다
차원이 더 높은
m by m 행렬
V^T(Transpose행렬) : A행렬보다
차원이 낮은
행렬
시그마 행렬 :
루트 람다로 이루어진 대각 행렬
(이 때 람다의 개수는 m by n의 n개와 값이 동일하다.)
여기서 우리는 람다(
λ)값에 왜 루트를 씌워야 하는지 의아해 할 수도 있다. 이는 처음에 SVD를 언급하면서 강조했던 Point부분과 연관이 있다. 즉,
A행렬보다 차원이 높고 낮은 행렬 각 1개를 서로 곱해주었다.
이 두 행렬을 곱합으로써
벡터길이(k)도 두 번 곱해진 것
이다. 우리는 Point라고 말했던 부분에서
SVD는 벡터의 방향을 바꿀지언정 길이(양)는 절대 변하지 않는다고 했다.
따라서 이를 맞춰주기 위해서
벡터의 길이를 두번 곱함(k제곱)에서 루트를 씌워주어 원래의 길이로 변환시켜주는 것
이다.
다음은 SVD의 종류이다. 크게 Full SVD와 Reduced SVD가 존재하는데 보통
Reduced SVD가 더 자주 활용
된다. Reduced SVD는
Thin SVD, Compact SVD, Truncated SVD
로 나누어 진다. 다음 그림을 보면서 각각의 종류를 이해해보자.
SVD의 종류
Full SVD는 딱히 설명할 부분이 없어 바로 Reduced SVD의 종류들에 대해 알아보자.
Thin
SVD : <그림3>에 해당하며
빨간색으로 쳐진 부분은 0이 될 부분
이기 때문에 해당 부분을 모두 없애버리고 SVD(3개의 행렬 내적연산)를 하는 종류이다. 그래서 원래의 행렬 A로 복구시키기 위해서는 없애버린 부분을 0으로만 채우면 된다.
Compact
SVD : <그림4>에 해당하며 Thin SVD와 마찬가지로
빨간색 부분이 0이 될 부분
이기 때문에 모두 없애버리고 SVD를 하는 종류이다. 원래의 행렬 A로 복구하는 방법은 Thin SVD 복구방법과 동일하다.
Truncated
SVD : <그림5>에 해당하며 다른 SVD와는 달리
0이 아닌 부분도 없애버리는 것이 특징
이다. 따라서
원래의 행렬 A로 완전한 복구가 힘들다.
그렇다면
Truncated
SVD는 왜 활용할까? 바로
이미지나 영상을 전달할 때 용량을 줄이기 위해 자주 사용
된다. 밑의 그림을 보자.
Truncated SVD를 활용한 이미지 변환
왼쪽의 원본 사진을 오른쪽 위는 Truncated SVD를 적용하지 않고 모든 요소를 살린 이미지, 오른쪽 아래는 Truncated SVD를 적용해 약간 흐릿하게 보이는 이미지를 볼 수 있다.
Truncated SVD
는 이처럼 0값이 아닌 요소들을 삭제할 때 이미지나 동영상에서 중요한 시각적 정보를 담고 있는것이 아닌 디테일하고 짜잘짜잘(?)한 정보들을 없애는 것
이다.
아까 SVD 종류라고 되어있는 자료사진의 Truncated SVD를 보자. SVD의 시그마(
Σ)행렬 부분을 보면
왼쪽 위에는 주로 중요한 정보
를 담고 있어 그 부분만을 살리지만
오른쪽 아래는 주로 디테일한 정보
가 들어있어 해당 부분을 삭제하게 된다.
4. PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
다음은 PCA라고 불리는 주성분 분석에 대해서 알아보자. PCA는
보통 데이터의 분포에 대한 주성분 즉, 최적의 Feature 조합을 찾기 위한 방법
이다. 여기서 주성분이란, 우리가 앞서 2.Eigen Value Decomposition 목차에서 배웠던 것을 적용하여 일명
'새로운 축(관점)'으로 데이터를 바라보는 것
이다. 이렇게 PCA를 하는 목적을 최적의 Feature를 선택한다고 해서
'Feature Selection'
라 하거나 n개의 Feature를 n-1개이하의 Feature로 감소시킨다고 하여
'Feature Dimension Reduction'
이라고도 한다.
그렇다면 PCA를 어떻게 하는 걸까?
PCA는 어떻게 동작할까?
PCA는 Eigen value decomposition(고유값 분할)을 통해
새로 만든 '축(관점)'으로 데이터를 바라보는 것
이다. 위 그림처럼 왼쪽의
청록색 축
이였다가 오른쪽으로
노란색 축
으로 데이터를 바라보는 것이다. PCA를 구하는 구체적인 단계는 다음과 같다.
PCA를 구하는 구체적인 단계
우선 주어진
데이터들의 평균(중심)으로 원점을 가정
한다. 그리고 Eigen value Decomposition을 통해서
공분산행렬, 고유값, 고유벡터를 구하게
됬다. 이렇게 고유값 분할을 통해 얻게 된
새로운 다양한 축(고유벡터) 관점에서
가장 큰 분산을 가질 때의 축
을 기준으로 데이터를 바라보게 되는 것
이다.
#공분산 : 서로 다른 2개의 Feature가 서로 얼마나 상관성이 있는지 수치화한 값
#Feature가 m개일 때 공분산행렬은 m by m이다.
5. LDA (Linear Discriminant Analysis)
LDA는 기본적으로
클래스를 가장 잘 구분할 수 있는 새로운 축을 찾아주기 위함
이다. 아래 그림을 보자.
어떤 축이 클래스를 더 잘 구분했을까?
우선 그림 속 필기내용은 제껴두고 그래프 분포와 축만보고 어떤 축이 데이터를 더 잘 구분해준 것일까?
잘 모르겠다면 밑의 수식을 이해하고 다시 이 문제에 대한 답을 찾아가보자.
LDA의 수식
기본적으로 어떤 축이 더 잘 구분했는지에 대한 척도를 측정하기 위한 목적함수는 다음의 2가지 기준으로 구성된다.
두 클래스의 중심간의 거리 간격
각 클래스 내의 데이터들의 분산값
위 수식에서 2개의 클라스의 각 중심은 M0, M1으로 나타내어지는 평균값이다. 그리고 우리는 우리가 찾고자하는 벡터와 각 클래스의 중심값을 곱한값들을 m0, m1이라고 하자. 이제
m0와 m1간의 거리를 최대화
시켜야 한다.
이 때 또 고려할 사항으로는
각 클래스 데이터들 내의 분산값
들이다. 따라서 목적함수는 다음과 같이 정의된다.
" 두 클래스간 중심간의 거리 / 각 클래스 내 분산의 합 "
따라서 수식은 다음과 같아지며
분모
인
분산값은 최소화
시킬수록,
분자
인
거리값은 최대가 될수록
가장 잘 분류할 수 있는 축을 구하기 위한 목적함수가 정의된다.
LDA의 목적함수
이렇게 목적함수를 정의한 후, 편미분을 통해 고유값과 고유벡터를 구하게 되며 구한
고유벡터값은 각 클래스를 가장 잘 분류해줄 수 있는 새로운 축
이 된다.
5-1. LDA의 용도와 한계
용도 :
분류문제에 적용
(이진분류 이상도 가능)이 가능하다. 또한 새로운 축을 구한 것이므로
Feature Selection
의 기능도 갖고 있다.
한계 : 각 클래스의 중심에 데이터가 몰려있음을 가정하므로
'비선형 분포 데이터'에는 부적합
하다.
5-2. PCA와 LDA의 차이는?
그러면 이쯤에서 PCA와 LDA의 차이에 대해 명확히 짚고 넘어가자. 다음 그림을 보고 각 차이에 대해 알아보자.
PCA vs LDA
PCA
: 데이터가
넓게 분포(분산이 큼)되어 있도록 하는 새로운 축
을 찾음.
LDA
: 클래스들을
가장 잘 구분할 수 있는 새로운 축
을 찾음.

title: [ML] LDA(선형판별분석)와 SVD(특이값 분할) 구현하기
description:
Why this lesson appears here:
This lesson fills the gap between intuitive model talk and the matrix-vector language used by modern ML implementations.

Knowledge bridge:
If the original article jumps directly into procedures or formulas, treat this lesson as both a preserved source note and a guided connection to the surrounding curriculum. Read the source details, then link them back to the core question of what assumptions, representations, or evaluation criteria make the method work.

Original article content preserved below:

이번 포스팅에서는
Linear Discriminant Analysis(LDA)인 선형판별분석과 Singular Value Decomposition(SVD)인 특이값 분할을 어떻게 구현할 수 있는지
에 대해 살펴보려고 한다. 본 포스팅에서는 개념에 대해서는 간단히 다루므로 보다 깊숙한 개념은
여기
를 참고하자.
목차는 다음과 같다.
1. LDA 구현해보기
2. SVD 구현해보기
1. LDA 구현해보기
LDA는 PCA와 비슷하게 입력
데이터셋을 저차원 공간으로 축소
하는 기법이다. 하지만 PCA와는 다르게 LDA는
지도학습의 분류문제를 해결하기 수월하도록 클래스를 가장 잘 분류할 수 있는 선형을 최대한 잘 유지하는 축을 찾아준다
는 차이점이 있다. LDA에 대한 목적함수나 수식에 대해서는
해당링크
를 참고하자.
LDA는 Scikit-learn에서 API로 제공을 하고 있다. 간단한 데이터에 적용해보자.
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
iris = load_iris()
#Scaling features
scaler = StandardScaler()
iris_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(iris.data)
# PCA와 유사하게 축소할 Components 수를 지정하자.
lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=2)
# LDA는 특이하게 fit 함수를 호출 시 종속변수(y값)을 넣어준다.
# 왜냐하면 클래스를 최대한 잘 분류할 수 있는 축을 찾아내기 위함이다.
# 그래서 종속변수값을 알고 있는 상태에서 모델링이 진행되기 때문에 지도학습 분류문제에 사용된다.
lda.fit(iris_scaled, iris.target)
# Scaling된 feature를 LDA활용해 차원축소시키기
iris_lda = lda.transform(iris_scaled)
print(iris_lda.shape)
LDA를 적용하여 차원 축소한 후의 feature를 기반으로 클래스값에 따른 데이터들의 산포도를 시각화해서 관찰해보자.
# 차원 축소시킨 후 데이터들의 산포도 살펴보기
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
lda_columns = ['lda_com1', 'lda_com2']
iris_df = pd.DataFrame(data=iris_lda, columns=lda_columns)
iris_df['target'] = iris.target
markers = ['^', 's', 'o']
for i, marker in enumerate(markers):
x_axis_data = iris_df[iris_df['target']==i]['lda_com1']
y_axis_data = iris_df[iris_df['target']==i]['lda_com2']
plt.scatter(x=x_axis_data, y=y_axis_data, marker=marker,
label=iris.target_names[i])
plt.legend()
plt.xlabel('lda_com1')
plt.ylabel('lda_com2')
plt.show()
클래스값에 따른 데이터들의 산포도
2. SVD 구현하기
SVD는
직각행렬에 적용
할 수 있는 분해방법이다. SVD의 종류에는 여러가지가 있는데 자세한 종류는
여기
를 참고하자. SVD는
Numpy, Scipy, Scikit-learn
라이브러리에서 각기의 방식으로 SVD의 API를 제공한다.
먼저,
아무것도 축소하는 것 없이 단순히 분할만 하며 원본 행렬로 복구가 가능한 Full SVD
를 구현하는 코드를 살펴보자.
# numpy의 svd 모듈
import numpy as np
from numpy.linalg import svd
# 4 by 4 행렬생성
np.random.seed(42)
a = np.random.randn(4,4)
print(np.round(a, 3))
# 반환된 분해된 행렬 확인해보기
# 디폴트 SVD는 Full SVD임
U, Sigma, Vt = svd(a)
print(U.shape, Sigma.shape, Vt.shape)
print('U matrix \n', np.round(U,3))
# Sigma 행렬은 1차원으로 도출되는데 이는 0이아닌 대각행렬의 요소값을 제외한 0값들은 출력을 안하기 때문.
print('Sigma matrix \n', np.round(Sigma, 3))
print('Vt matrix \n', np.round(Vt, 3))
# 분해된 행렬 다시 원상복구해보기
# Sigma 행렬의 대각요소 제외한 0부분 다시 원상복구 시키기
Sigma_mat = np.diag(Sigma)
# np.dot은 행렬끼리 내적시키는 연산
a_ = np.dot(np.dot(U, Sigma_mat), Vt)
print(np.round(a_, 3))
다음은 차원을 축소하지만
0인 값들만 축소하므로 원본 행렬로 복구가 가능한 Compact SVD
이다.
# Compact SVD 수행해보기
# 데이터 의존도가 서로 존재하는 행렬 임의로 생성
a[2] = a[0] + a[1]
a[3] = a[0]
print(np.round(a,3))
# SVD 분할 수행
U, Sigma, Vt = svd(a)
print(U.shape, Sigma.shape, Vt.shape)
print(np.round(Sigma, 3))
# 분할 후 다시 복원
U_ = U[:, :2]
Sigma_ = np.diag(Sigma[:2])
Vt_ = Vt[:2]
print(U_.shape, Sigma_.shape, Vt_.shape)
a_ = np.dot(np.dot(U_, Sigma_), Vt_)
print(np.round(a_, 3))
다음은
0이 아닌 요소값들(주로 데이터에서 중요하지 않은 부분)을 제거하여 축소하기 때문에 원본 행렬로 복구하기는 힘든 Truncated SVD
구현코드를 살펴보자. 먼저 Scipy 라이브러리를 이용한 코드다.
# Truncated SVD 수행하기
# Truncated SVD는 Scipy의 spares의 svds 사용
# 일반 SVD는
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse.linalg import svds
from scipy.linalg import svd
np.random.seed(12)
matrix = np.random.random((6,6))
print('원본 행렬\n', np.round(matrix,3))
# full_matrices=True면 U를 (M,M) Vt를 (N,N)으로 분할하고
# full_matrices=False면 U를 (M,k) Vt를 (k,N)으로 분할한다.
# 이 때, k= M,N 중 최소값임.
U, Sigma, Vt = svd(matrix, full_matrices=False)
print('분해 행렬 차원', U.shape, Sigma.shape, Vt.shape)
print('Sigma값', np.round(Sigma,3))
# Truncated SVD
# 특이값(대각행렬의 대각값들) 몇개로 할지 사전정의.
num_comp=4
U_tr, Sigma_tr, Vt_tr = svds(matrix, k=num_comp)
print('Truncated SVD 적용 후 행렬차원',U_tr.shape,Sigma_tr.shape,
Vt_tr.shape)
print('Truncated SVD 적용 후 특이값', np.round(Sigma_tr, 3))
# 다시 원본 행렬로 복구 시도해보기
matrix_tr = np.dot(np.dot(U_tr, np.diag(Sigma_tr)), Vt_tr)
print('원본 행렬 복구 시도한 행렬', np.round(matrix_tr, 3))
원본 행렬과 복구한 후 행렬 요소들을 비교해보면 값들이 비슷한 수치들이지만 Full, Compact SVD와는 달리 100%
일치하지 않는 것
을 볼 수 있다.
Truncated SVD는 원본 행렬을 똑같이 복구시킬 수 없다.
다음은 Scikit-learn 라이브러리를 이용한 코드이다.
# Scikit-learn에서 제공하는 Truncated SVD이용
from sklearn.decomposition import TruncatedSVD, PCA
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
iris = load_iris()
iris_features = iris.data
# 2개의 특이값으로 분할
tsvd = TruncatedSVD(n_components=2)
tsvd.fit(iris_features)
iris_tsvd = tsvd.transform(iris_features)
# 분할 후 데이터 산포도 시각화
plt.scatter(x=iris_tsvd[:,0], y=iris_tsvd[:,1], c=iris.target)
plt.xlabel('Comp1')
plt.ylabel('Comp2')
Truncated SVD 적용후 데이터 분포
다음은 추가적인 내용인데, 바로
NMF(Non-negative Matrix Factorization)
에 대한 내용이다. NMF는
Non-negative
에서 유추해볼 수 있는 것처럼 원본
행렬 내의 모든 요소값들이 모두 0값 이상의 양수
일 때 좀 더 간단하게 양수 행렬로 분할할 수 있는 기법이다. Scikit-learn에서 API를 제공하고 있으며 간단하게 적용 후 데이터를 시각화하면 다음과 같은 결과를 얻게 된다.
# NMF(Non-negative Matrix Factorization)
from sklearn.decomposition import NMF
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
iris = load_iris()
iris_features = iris.data
nmf = NMF(n_components=2)
iris_nmf = nmf.fit_transform(iris_features)
plt.scatter(x=iris_nmf[:,0], y=iris_nmf[:,1],
c=iris.target)
plt.xlabel('NMF comp1')
plt.ylabel('NMF comp2')
NMF 적용 후 데이터의 분포도
지금까지 LDA와 여러가지 종류의 SVD를 구현하는 방법에 대해 알아보았다. 끝으로
PCA, LDA, 다양한 SVD들
은 모두 차원을 축소 즉, feature들을 축소시킴으로써
내재된(Latent) feature들을 새로 만드는 특징으로서 Feature Extraction이 기본

title: 선형성(Linearity) 정의 및 1차연립방정식의 의미
description:
Why this lesson appears here:
This lesson fills the gap between intuitive model talk and the matrix-vector language used by modern ML implementations.

Knowledge bridge:
If the original article jumps directly into procedures or formulas, treat this lesson as both a preserved source note and a guided connection to the surrounding curriculum. Read the source details, then link them back to the core question of what assumptions, representations, or evaluation criteria make the method work.

Original article content preserved below:

선형대수 카테고리에서는 한양대학교 KOCW 오픈강의 이상화 교수님의 선형대수 강의를 듣고 이에 대한 학습 포스팅을 남기려고 한다. 이번학기에 전공과목으로 배우기 시작한 머신러닝 과목에서 확률과 통계 개념도 등장했지만 모델에 따라 선형대수에 관한 개념도 많이 등장해서 개인적으로
선형대수학
을 공부하려고 한다.
첫 포스팅은 선형대수의 '
선형성'이라는 것에 대한 정의
와
1차연립방정식의 의미
에 대해 알아보자.
1. 선형성(Linearity)
선형성의 정의
우선 '선형'이라는 말은
"특정 함수나 Operation(연산)이 Linear(선형적)하다."
라는 말에 사용될 수 있다. "특정함수나 연산이 Linear하다"라고 하기 위해서는 두 가지 조건을 만족해야 한다.
Superposition(중첩)
:
f(x1+x2) = f(x1) + f(x2)
라는 식을 만족해야 한다.
Homogeneity(동종)
:
f(ax) = af(x)
식을 만족해야 한다. 이 때 a는 constant로서 상수이다.
따라서 위 두개의 조건을 모두 만족하게 되면
f(a1x1+a2x2) = a1f(x1) + a2f(x2)
가 되게 된다.
그리고 "특정 함수가 Linear 하다" 라고 할 수 있는 기본적인 성질이 있는데 그것은 바로
'원점을 지나는' 함수
이다. 위 그림의 y=mx 일 때와 y=mx+n 이라는 원점을 지나고 지나지 않는 각각의 예시를 보도록 하자. 참고로 알아두어야 할 점은
원점을 지나지 않는 y=mx+n 함수에서 m이라는 기울기(x변화율에대한 y변화율)는 "Linear 하다"
라고 할 수 있다.
다음은 함수가 아닌 연산의 일종인 '미분, 적분' 일 때와 '행렬'일 때의 Linear 성질을 살펴보자. 기본적인 '중첩'과 '동종'의 성질은 비슷하고
식의 형태에 집중하면서 밑의 그림을 보면 된다.
연산과 행렬의 Linearity
이제 우리는 행렬을 자주 다룰텐데 우선 행렬에 대한 기본적인 표기법 부터 알고가자. 이것은 추후의 필기 내용을 이해하는 데에 도움이 될 것이다.
행렬의 기본 표기법
우선 선형대수에서의 행렬은
'행 벡터'
가 아닌
'열 벡터'
를 다룰 것이다. 두 개의 관계는 서로
Transpose(전치)한 관계
이다. Transpose란
행과 열을 서로 바꿔주는 것
을 말하는 데 위 그림의 오른쪽 예시를 참고하면 이해가 수월할 것이다.
2. Linear Combination(선형 결합)
다음은 중요한 Linear Combination에 관한 내용이다. 밑의 그림에서 V, W는 열 벡터이며 알파와 베타값은 상수(Constant)이다.
선형 결합을 알아보자.
우리는 위 그림에서 주목해야 할 점은
V, W라는 열 벡터를 하나의 행렬로 감싸주고 알파와 베타값을 곱해줌으로써 맨 오른쪽 식과같이 '선형결합'의 형태가 된다는 점을 인지
하고 있어야 한다는 것이다.
3. 행렬과 항등원, 그리고 역원은 무엇인가?
고등학교 시절 행렬, 항등원, 역원에 대해서 배웠었지만 기억이 희미했다. 다행히 교수님께서 이에 대한 개념을 간략적으로 가르쳐주셨고 간단하게 개념을 짚고 넘어가자.
행렬, 항등원, 역원
우선 m by n 이라는 행렬이 있다고 하자. 이를 n by l 이라는 하나의 행렬을 곱하게 되면 m by l 이라는 행렬이 나오게 된다. 이 때
곱셈 연산을 했던 두 개의 행렬 끼리는 [ m by n 의 열에 해당하는 n값 = m by l 의 행에 해당하는 n값 ] 이 같아야 한다.
단, 이 때
서로 교환법칙이 성립하지 않는다.
그럼
항등원
과
역원
에 대해서 알아보자.
항등원
: 고등학교 시절 E라는 기호로 자주 사용했으며 여기에서는 주로 Identity Element의 I를 따서
I라고 표기
를 하게 된다. 그리고 위 그림과 같이
대각행렬이 1로만 이루어져있는 것을 말하며
임의의 행렬 A에 항등원 I를 곱하면 자기 자신 행렬인 A가 나오게 된다. 이 때 교환법칙이 성립한다.
역원
:
임의의 행렬 A에 '어떤 행렬'을 곱했을 때 I라는 항등원 행렬이 나오는 것
을 말한다. 역원을 구하는 공식은 위의 그림과 같다. 하지만 위 예시에서는 2 by 2행렬을 예시로 들었지만 차원이 높아지게 되면 적용했던 역원을 구하는 공식을 사용하지 못하게 된다. 이로 인해 추후에 소개할
'가우스 소거법'
이 등장하게 된다.
4. 벡터의 연산과 함수에서의 내적
두 개의 벡터를 더하고, 뺀것, 그리고 곱하는 연산의 결과값이 어떻게 도출되는지 밑의 그림을 보면서 이해하자.
벡터의
합
: 두 개의 벡터를 사용해
평행사변형의 원리를 적용
하여 계산한다.
벡터의
차이(뺄셈)
: 두 개의 벡터 사이의 거리를 측정하는 것처럼 계산.
(밑에 그림 참조)
벡터의
곱
:
inner product라는 내적방법을 사용
하는데 공식은 밑의 그림과 같아진다.
벡터의 연산과 함수의 내적
내적방법은 함수에서도 사용
할 수 있는데 f1(t), f2(t) 라는 두 개의 함수가 있다고 가정하자. 이를 벡터에 적용해본다면 무수히 많은 f1(t), f2(t)의 값들이 f1(t), f2(t)의 각각 벡터들의 element(요소)로 정의할 수 있다. 그리고 이 두 개의 벡터를 곱한것을
적분하는 방식으로 내적을 할 수 있게 된다.
5. Gauss Elimination(가우스 소거법)
아까 역원을 구하는 방식에서 잠깐 언급했던 가우스 소거법에 대해서 알아보자. 우선적으로 말하면
가우스 소거법
은 어떠한
'공식'
이 아닌
'절차'를 의미
한다는 것을 알아두자.
가우스 소거법은 선형(Linear) 연립 방정식을 풀기 위한 절차
(방법)으로 정의할 수 있다. 밑의 예시를 보면서 우리가 고등학교 시절 자주 알고 있는 방법으로서 row form 형태와 행렬, 그리고 벡터의 형태순으로 알아보자. 포인트는 일차식과 행렬을 이용하는
row form 방식
은
두 개의 교점을 찾는 것
이지만,
벡터를 이용
할 때는
열 벡터(Column vectors)들의 선형결합을 찾는 것
이다.
가우스 소거법의 원리
위와 같이 2가지의 방법이 있지만
row form
을 이용하는 것은 더 높은 차원의 문제를 해결할 때는 한계가 있다. 따라서 위대한 수학자 가우스는
벡터를 이용하는 것이 더 많은 범위의 문제를 풀 수 있다
고 주장했다.
그렇다면 이번엔 벡터를 이용해서 3차원 벡터의 예시를 살펴보자.
밑의 그림과 같이 3차원 벡터가 존재하고 이는 선형결합(Linear Combination)으로 바꿔줄 수 있다.
#이 때 변수 u,v w의 계수들이 서로 순서가 바뀌어도 우리가 구하려고 하는 값인 u,v w값들은 동일한 점을 알아두자.

title: 1차 연립방정식과 가우스 소거법(Gauss Elimination)
description:
Why this lesson appears here:
This lesson fills the gap between intuitive model talk and the matrix-vector language used by modern ML implementations.

Knowledge bridge:
If the original article jumps directly into procedures or formulas, treat this lesson as both a preserved source note and a guided connection to the surrounding curriculum. Read the source details, then link them back to the core question of what assumptions, representations, or evaluation criteria make the method work.

Original article content preserved below:

이번 포스팅에서는 Singular Case에 대해 알아보고 저번 포스팅에서 소개했었던 가우스 소거법의 구체적인 절차(방법)에 대해서 소개하려고 한다. 목차는 다음과 같다.
1. Singular Case란?
2. Gauss Elimination(가우스 소거법) 절차
1. Singular Case란?
우선 정의부터 하자면 Singular Case란
Unique한 해를 가지지 않을 때
를 말하며 두 가지의 Case가 존재한다.
No solution
: 해가
존재하지 않아서
해결책이 없는 경우이다.
Infinite solution
: 해가
무수히 많아서
해결책이 무한한 개수인 경우이다.
다음 그림을 보면서
row form(도형, 직선)일 때
와
Column form(벡터)일 때
두 가지 예시를 나누어서 살펴보자.
Singular Case란, 해가 없거나 해가 무수히 많을 때를 말한다.
< row form (도형, 직선)일 경우 >
No solution
: 서로 평행할 때
Infinite solution
: 서로 겹칠(Overlap) 때
< Column form (벡터)일 경우 >
No solution
: 서로 벡터가 평행할 때
Infinite solution
: 같은 평면상의 a라는 벡터를 구할 때
Column form(벡터)일 경우
텍스트상으로 이해가 되지 않는다면 위 필기의 벡터에 관한 그림을 보면서 이해해보자.
2. Gauss Elimination(가우스 소거법)
다음은 가우스 소거법에 대한 구체적인 방법이다. 연립방정식이든 행렬이든 어떤 형태로 나타낼 때는
"계수가 0이 아닌 변수를 가장 먼저(왼쪽)에 두고 계산을 해야한다"
는 점이 중요하다.
가우스 소거법의 구체적인 절차
가우스 소거법으로 문제를 해결하기 위해서는 또 하나의 조건이 필요한데, 이른바
'Pivot'이라는 특정 변수(그림 속에서는 u, v, w)의 계수가 non-zero(0이 아닌)이어야 한다는 것
이다. 위 그림의
파란색 동그라미로 쳐진 부분
을 보면 변수를 순차적으로
u -> v -> w

Why is linear algebra unavoidable in ML?

Because it only matters for physics simulations.
Because modern models no longer use matrix operations.
explanations: Correct. Linear algebra is the operational language of model computation.
Its relevance is much broader than physics.
Modern ML systems are saturated with matrix operations.
quizzes.answerReason: This is the bridge from qualitative intuition to the actual computational objects models manipulate.

quizzes.question: What skill should you gain from this lesson?
options: The ability to read model equations and code as transformations over spaces, dimensions, and basis representations.
A habit of ignoring dimensions and hoping operations work out.
A belief that matrices only exist in textbook proofs.

Dimension discipline is core to debugging.
ML code uses these ideas constantly.

title: Random Variables and the CDF
description: A random variable maps outcomes to numbers so we can reason about uncertainty algebraically instead of only through verbal cases. Its cumulative distribution function, or CDF, gives the probability that the variable is less than or equal to a threshold. This matters because threshold probabilities, quantiles, and inverse sampling all start from the CDF. A common pitfall is confusing the probability at a point with the cumulative probability up to that point.
code:
values = [1, 2, 2, 4, 5]
threshold = 2
cdf = sum(x <= threshold for x in values) / len(values)
print(cdf)

quizzes.question: What fraction of the sample is less than or equal to the threshold?
What does a CDF at value x represent?
options: The probability that the random variable is less than or equal to x.
The probability density exactly at x.
The average value of the random variable above x.
explanations: Correct. The CDF accumulates probability up to the threshold.
That describes a density or point mass, not the cumulative function.
A CDF is about probability mass, not conditional averages.
quizzes.answerReason: The CDF answers a threshold question: how much probability has accumulated by x.

quizzes.question: What is the main pitfall when using a CDF?
options: Mixing up cumulative probability with probability at a single value.
Thinking the CDF must always decrease.
Assuming the CDF can exceed 1 if the sample is large.
explanations: Correct. This confusion is especially common when moving between discrete and continuous cases.
A CDF is non-decreasing by definition.
A CDF is always between 0 and 1.
quizzes.answerReason: Point probability and cumulative probability are different objects, and mixing them breaks later reasoning.

title: Continuous Random Variables and the PDF
description: For a continuous random variable, probabilities live on intervals rather than at exact points, so we use a probability density function, or PDF. The PDF tells you where probability is concentrated, and areas under the curve correspond to probabilities. This matters because many losses, likelihoods, and noise models assume continuous variables. A common pitfall is reading the height of a PDF as a probability instead of remembering that probability comes from area.

quizzes.question: What probability is assigned to an interval of width 0.5 under this uniform density?
What does a PDF value f(x) mean?
options: It is a density whose area over an interval gives probability.
It is the probability that X equals exactly x.
It is always between 0 and 1 because it is a probability.
explanations: Correct. Density becomes probability only after integration over a region.
For continuous variables, exact-point probability is typically zero.
A density can exceed 1 as long as the total area is 1.
quizzes.answerReason: The PDF is not itself a probability mass at a point. It is a rate of probability per unit of x.

quizzes.question: Which statement is true for continuous random variables?
options: P(a <= X <= b) is found by integrating the PDF over [a, b].
P(X = a) is usually the main quantity of interest.
Changing units never affects the density.
explanations: Correct. Interval probability is the central operation in the continuous case.
Exact-point probability is usually zero.
Densities rescale when units change.
quizzes.answerReason: Continuous probability is fundamentally about intervals, not isolated points.

title: Joint and Conditional Densities
description: A joint density describes how two variables vary together, while a conditional density describes one variable after fixing information about the other. These ideas matter because prediction often means turning a joint relationship into a conditional one. They also support independence tests, graphical models, and Bayesian updates. A common pitfall is treating dependence as if each variable could still be modeled in isolation without loss.

quizzes.question: What is P(X=1 | Y=1) rounded to two decimals?
Why are conditional distributions central in ML?
options: Because prediction usually asks for the target distribution after observing features.
Because conditionals are only needed in pure Bayesian statistics.
Because a conditional distribution is always the same as the marginal distribution.
explanations: Correct. Classification and regression both rely on conditional structure.
Conditionals appear in mainstream supervised learning as well.
Conditioning often changes the distribution dramatically.
quizzes.answerReason: Supervised learning is largely about modeling Y given X, which is a conditional view of uncertainty.

quizzes.question: If X and Y are independent, what must be true?
options: Their joint distribution factors into the product of their marginals.
Their conditional distribution is undefined.
They must have the same mean.
explanations: Correct. Factorization is the defining probability statement for independence.
Conditional distributions still exist under independence.
Equal means are unrelated to independence.
quizzes.answerReason: Independence is about factorization of probability, not about matching summary statistics.

title: Sums of Continuous Variables and Convolution
description: When independent random variables are added, the distribution of the sum is found by convolution. This matters because noise terms, waiting times, and aggregated signals are often sums of smaller random effects. Convolution also appears in signal processing and deep learning, though the interpretation differs by context. A common pitfall is assuming the sum keeps the same distribution family without checking the actual algebra or independence assumptions.
code:
x = [0.5, 1.0, 1.5]
y = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
sums = [a + b for a, b in zip(x, y)]
print(sum(sums) / len(sums))

quizzes.question: What is the average of the pairwise sums?
What does convolution answer in probability?
options: How the distribution of a sum is formed from the component distributions.
How to sort observations before estimating a mean.
How to convert a continuous variable into a discrete one.
explanations: Correct. Convolution is the rule for combining independent additive randomness.
Sorting is unrelated.
Convolution combines distributions; it does not discretize variables.
quizzes.answerReason: The point of convolution is to move from parts to the distribution of their total.

quizzes.question: What assumption is commonly needed when convolving two random variables?
options: Independence of the variables being added.
Equal means and equal variances.
A Gaussian distribution for each variable.
explanations: Correct. The standard convolution formula assumes independence.
Equal means are not required.
Many families can be convolved; Gaussian is not mandatory.
quizzes.answerReason: Without independence, the joint structure must be handled explicitly instead of using the simple convolution rule.

title: Geometric Distribution, Error Models, and Conditional Expectation
description: The geometric distribution models the number of trials until the first success in repeated independent Bernoulli trials. Conditional expectation extends that idea by asking for the average outcome after some information is observed. This matters because many estimators and forecasts are best understood as conditional expectations under an error model. A common pitfall is forgetting that the geometric model assumes a constant success probability from trial to trial.
code:
p = 0.25
expected_trials = 1 / p
print(expected_trials)

quizzes.question: What is the expected number of trials until first success?
When is a geometric distribution a natural model?
options: When repeated trials are independent and each trial has the same success probability.
When outcomes are continuous and symmetric around a mean.
When counts of events in fixed time windows must allow arbitrarily many simultaneous categories.
explanations: Correct. That repeated-trial setup is exactly what geometric models describe.
That sounds closer to a normal-style continuous model.
That does not describe the waiting-time-to-first-success setting.
quizzes.answerReason: The geometric model is about waiting time under repeated identical Bernoulli trials.

quizzes.question: Why is conditional expectation important in prediction?
options: Because many prediction targets are best viewed as expected outcomes given the observed information.
Because it guarantees zero error on every example.
Because it removes the need for a probability model.
explanations: Correct. Regression functions are often conditional expectations in disguise.
It is an average target, not a guarantee for each case.
Conditional expectation is defined inside a probabilistic model.
quizzes.answerReason: A lot of prediction theory becomes clearer once you recognize the target as E[Y | X].

title: Conditional Probability and Bayes' Rule
description: Conditional probability updates uncertainty after new evidence is observed, and Bayes' rule gives the algebra for reversing conditions. This matters in diagnostics, classification, filtering, and Bayesian inference, where evidence changes what you should believe about hidden states. A common pitfall is ignoring the base rate and focusing only on how accurate a test seems in isolation.
code:
prior = 0.01
sensitivity = 0.95
false_positive_rate = 0.10
posterior = (sensitivity * prior) / ((sensitivity * prior) + (false_positive_rate * (1 - prior)))
print(round(posterior, 3))

quizzes.question: What is the posterior probability after a positive test?
What does Bayes' rule fundamentally do?
options: It updates prior beliefs using observed evidence.
It proves that every conditional probability is symmetric.
It removes the need to model false positives and false negatives.
explanations: Correct. Bayes' rule combines prior belief and likelihood evidence.
Conditionals are generally not symmetric.
Error rates are part of the likelihood and remain essential.
quizzes.answerReason: Bayes' rule is a disciplined method for belief revision, not a shortcut around modeling assumptions.

quizzes.question: What is the classic base-rate mistake?
options: Treating a high-quality test as if a positive result must imply a high posterior probability even when the event is very rare.
Using more data to reduce uncertainty.
Conditioning on evidence after observing it.
explanations: Correct. Rare events can still yield many false alarms relative to true positives.
Using more data is usually helpful, not a mistake.
Conditioning on evidence is the correct operation.
quizzes.answerReason: Ignoring the prior prevalence leads to badly misread posteriors.

title: Bernoulli, Binomial, and Chebyshev's Inequality
description: Bernoulli variables model one success-failure event, while the binomial distribution models the count of successes across repeated Bernoulli trials. Chebyshev's inequality gives a broad distribution-free bound on how far values can fall from the mean. This matters because it separates what you can guarantee from what you only assume. A common pitfall is expecting loose worst-case bounds like Chebyshev to behave like sharp Gaussian tail probabilities.
code:
p = 0.6
n = 5
expected_successes = n * p
print(expected_successes)

quizzes.question: What is the expected number of successes?
What is the difference between Bernoulli and binomial models?
options: Bernoulli models one trial; binomial models the count of successes across multiple independent Bernoulli trials.
Bernoulli is continuous; binomial is discrete.
Bernoulli ignores probability; binomial uses it.
explanations: Correct. The binomial distribution is built from repeated Bernoulli trials.
Both are discrete distributions.
Both distributions are defined by probability.
quizzes.answerReason: The binomial model is the repeated-trial extension of the Bernoulli case.

quizzes.question: Why is Chebyshev's inequality useful?
options: It gives a guaranteed variance-based bound even when the exact distribution is unknown.
It only works for normal distributions.
It always provides tighter bounds than specialized tail formulas.
explanations: Correct. Its strength is generality, not tightness.
It is distribution-agnostic as long as variance exists.
General bounds are often looser than model-specific ones.
quizzes.answerReason: Chebyshev is valuable because it works under weak assumptions.

title: Bernoulli Distribution
description: A Bernoulli distribution models a single binary event such as click or no click, fraud or no fraud, positive or negative. It is the simplest probabilistic building block behind logistic regression, binary classification metrics, and coin-flip style reasoning. This matters because many larger models reduce to repeated Bernoulli outcomes at training or evaluation time. A common pitfall is treating numeric labels like 0 and 1 as ordinary continuous values instead of probabilities over two outcomes.
code:
p = 0.7
expected_value = 1 * p + 0 * (1 - p)
variance = p * (1 - p)
print(round(expected_value, 2))
print(round(variance, 2))

quizzes.question: What are the mean and variance of this Bernoulli variable?
What kind of outcome does a Bernoulli variable represent?
options: One binary success-failure event.
A count of successes across many trials.
A continuous symmetric measurement.
explanations: Correct. Bernoulli is the one-trial binary model.
That is the binomial setting.
That is not a Bernoulli variable.
quizzes.answerReason: Bernoulli is the smallest useful model for binary uncertainty.

quizzes.question: Why does Bernoulli modeling show up so often in ML?
options: Because many labels, events, and threshold decisions are binary.
Because all classification problems are actually one-dimensional regression problems.
Because Bernoulli variables do not require probabilities.
explanations: Correct. Clicks, conversions, detections, and yes-no outcomes are everywhere.
That overstates the relationship and misses multiclass structure.
Probability is the defining parameter of a Bernoulli model.
quizzes.answerReason: A large amount of applied ML is built on binary events, even when the surrounding system is complex.

title: Binomial Distribution
description: The binomial distribution models how many successes occur in a fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials with constant success probability. It matters for A/B tests, quality control, conversion modeling, and confidence intervals for proportions. A common pitfall is using it when trials are not independent or when the success rate changes across trials.
code:
from math import comb
n = 4
k = 2
p = 0.5
prob = comb(n, k) * (p ** k) * ((1 - p) ** (n - k))
print(prob)

quizzes.question: What is the probability of exactly 2 successes?
When is a binomial model appropriate?
options: When you count successes across a fixed number of independent trials with the same success probability.
When each observation can take any real value.
When the number of trials is unknown and potentially unbounded within an interval.
explanations: Correct. Those are the defining assumptions of the binomial distribution.
That is a continuous setting.
That sounds more like a count-process model such as Poisson.
quizzes.answerReason: The binomial model is a fixed-trial counting model.

quizzes.question: What is the main pitfall when applying a binomial model to real data?
options: Forgetting that changing probabilities or dependent trials break the model assumptions.
Using a success probability between 0 and 1.
Counting the number of observed successes.
explanations: Correct. Real systems often have drift, dependence, or segmentation effects.
A probability between 0 and 1 is required, not a problem.
That is the quantity the model is built for.
quizzes.answerReason: The binomial model is simple and useful, but only under its repeated-trial assumptions.

title: Multinomial Distribution
description: The multinomial distribution generalizes the binomial case to more than two categories. It models category counts across repeated trials when each trial ends in exactly one class. This matters for language modeling, bag-of-words counts, multiclass labels, and confusion analysis. A common pitfall is forgetting that the class counts are linked because they must sum to the total number of trials.
code:
counts = [3, 2, 1]
print(sum(counts))
print(counts.index(max(counts)))

quizzes.question: What does the code print about the category counts?
What does a multinomial distribution model?
options: Counts across multiple mutually exclusive categories over repeated trials.
One continuous measurement with Gaussian noise.
The waiting time until the first success.
explanations: Correct. It is the multiclass extension of the binomial idea.
That is not a multinomial setting.
That describes the geometric distribution.
quizzes.answerReason: Multinomial structure appears whenever each trial chooses one label from several classes.

quizzes.question: Why are category counts dependent in a multinomial sample?
options: Because increasing one category count leaves fewer trials for the others once the total is fixed.
Because each category has to have the same probability.
Because multinomial models do not allow zero counts.
explanations: Correct. The fixed total couples the counts together.
Class probabilities can differ.
Zero counts are perfectly possible.
quizzes.answerReason: The counts are constrained by the total number of trials, so they cannot vary independently.

title: Poisson Distribution
description: The Poisson distribution models counts of events in a fixed interval when events occur independently at an average rate. It matters for traffic, arrivals, incident counts, and sparse event modeling. It also explains why count data often have variance linked to the mean. A common pitfall is using Poisson when overdispersion or dependence makes the data much more variable than the model allows.
code:
rate_per_hour = 3
hours = 4
expected_events = rate_per_hour * hours
print(expected_events)

quizzes.question: How many events are expected over 4 hours at this rate?
What kind of data is Poisson designed for?
options: Counts of events over time, area, or space.
Binary single-trial outcomes only.
Continuous measurements with symmetric noise.
explanations: Correct. Poisson is the standard starting model for event counts.
That is Bernoulli territory.
That is closer to normal-style modeling.
quizzes.answerReason: Poisson is about counting events, not measuring continuous values.

quizzes.question: What is a warning sign that Poisson may be a poor fit?
options: The observed variance is much larger than the mean.
The data are recorded as counts.
The average rate is positive.
explanations: Correct. That overdispersion often signals dependence or unmodeled heterogeneity.
Counts are exactly the kind of data Poisson aims to model.
A positive rate is expected, not a problem.
quizzes.answerReason: Poisson imposes a specific mean-variance relationship that real data often violate.

title: Exponential and Erlang Distributions
description: The exponential distribution models the waiting time until one event occurs in a Poisson process, while the Erlang distribution models the waiting time until several events occur. These distributions matter for queues, survival modeling, and reliability analysis. They also connect counts over time to waiting times between events. A common pitfall is using an exponential model when the hazard rate is clearly not constant.
code:
rate = 2
expected_wait = 1 / rate
expected_wait_for_3_events = 3 / rate
print(expected_wait)
print(expected_wait_for_3_events)

quizzes.question: What are the expected waiting times for one event and for three events?
How are exponential and Erlang models related?
options: Exponential is the waiting time to one event; Erlang is the waiting time to several Poisson events.
They are unrelated and used for different variable types.
Erlang is only for binary outcomes.
explanations: Correct. Erlang is a multi-event waiting-time extension of the exponential idea.
They are closely related through Poisson processes.
Binary outcomes are not the right framing here.
quizzes.answerReason: These models are connected through repeated event arrivals in continuous time.

quizzes.question: What assumption makes the exponential model distinctive?
options: A constant event rate, which implies the memoryless property.
A fixed number of trials.
Symmetry around a mean.
explanations: Correct. Constant hazard is the key assumption behind exponential waiting times.
That is a binomial-style assumption.
Symmetry is not an exponential feature.
quizzes.answerReason: The memoryless behavior comes from a constant arrival or failure rate.

title: Exponential Distribution
description: The exponential distribution is a continuous model for waiting times when events occur at a constant average rate. It matters because it is mathematically simple, memoryless, and tightly connected to Poisson counting processes. It is often the first continuous lifetime model used in practice. A common pitfall is applying it to systems where the chance of failure changes over time.
code:
rate = 4
mean = 1 / rate
prob_wait_more_than_half = 2.718281828 ** (-rate * 0.5)
print(mean)
print(round(prob_wait_more_than_half, 3))

quizzes.question: What are the mean waiting time and the probability of waiting more than 0.5 units?
Why is the exponential distribution called memoryless?
options: The chance of waiting longer does not depend on how long you have already waited.
Its parameters are impossible to estimate from data.
It only remembers the most recent event.
explanations: Correct. Future waiting time under the model depends only on the constant rate, not on elapsed time.
The parameter is straightforward to estimate.
That is not what memoryless means in probability.
quizzes.answerReason: Memorylessness is a formal property of the waiting-time distribution, not a slogan.

quizzes.question: When is the exponential model a poor fit?
options: When failure risk grows as a machine ages.
When time is measured continuously.
When average waiting time is positive.
explanations: Correct. A changing hazard rate breaks the core assumption.
Continuous time is appropriate here.
A positive mean is expected.
quizzes.answerReason: If the hazard is not constant, the exponential model becomes structurally wrong.

title: Gamma, Beta, Chi-Square, t, and F Distributions
description: These distributions form a toolkit for modeling positive quantities, probabilities, scaled sums of squares, uncertainty in means, and variance ratios. They matter because many classical tests, confidence intervals, and Bayesian updates are built from them. Understanding the family relationships is more useful than memorizing isolated formulas. A common pitfall is learning the names without learning what kind of variable each distribution is meant to model.
code:
families = ["gamma: positive waiting times", "beta: probabilities", "t: mean with estimated variance"]
print(len(families))
print(families[1])

quizzes.question: What summary of the distribution families is printed?
Which distribution is naturally defined on the interval [0, 1]?
options: Beta
Gamma
Chi-square
explanations: Correct. Beta is a natural model for probabilities and proportions.
Gamma lives on positive real values.
Chi-square also lives on positive values.
quizzes.answerReason: Support matters. Matching the range of the variable is one of the first checks in distribution choice.

quizzes.question: Why is the t distribution important?
options: It accounts for uncertainty in the variance estimate when inferring a mean from finite data.
It is the exact distribution for all positive random variables.
It replaces the need for sample size considerations.
explanations: Correct. Heavier tails reflect extra uncertainty from estimated variance.
That is false.
Sample size still matters strongly.
quizzes.answerReason: The t distribution is a correction for finite-sample uncertainty, not a universal fallback.

title: Gamma Distribution
description: The gamma distribution models positive continuous quantities such as waiting times until multiple events or other skewed nonnegative variables. It matters in Bayesian modeling, queueing, reliability, and as a parent family containing special cases such as the exponential distribution. A common pitfall is using it on data that can take negative values or on variables whose shape is actually bounded above.
code:
shape = 3
rate = 2
mean = shape / rate
print(mean)

quizzes.question: What is the gamma mean for this shape-rate parameterization?
What kind of variable is gamma usually used for?
options: Positive continuous values, often with right skew.
Binary success-failure outcomes.
Probabilities constrained to lie between 0 and 1.
explanations: Correct. Gamma is a standard positive-support distribution.
That is Bernoulli territory.
That is a beta-style support.
quizzes.answerReason: The support of the gamma distribution is positive real numbers.

quizzes.question: Which statement is true?
options: The exponential distribution is a special case of the gamma family.
Gamma distributions are symmetric around zero.
Gamma variables can take any negative value as long as the mean is positive.
explanations: Correct. Exponential corresponds to a gamma distribution with a specific shape parameter.
Gamma distributions are typically skewed and positive-only.
Negative support is not allowed.
quizzes.answerReason: Family relationships matter because they let you reuse intuition across models.

title: Beta Distribution
description: The beta distribution is a flexible continuous distribution on the interval from 0 to 1, making it a natural model for probabilities and proportions. It matters in Bayesian inference because it updates cleanly with Bernoulli and binomial observations. It can represent confidence near 0, near 1, or around the middle depending on its parameters. A common pitfall is using beta for data that are not bounded between 0 and 1.
code:
alpha = 2
beta = 3
mean = alpha / (alpha + beta)
print(mean)

quizzes.question: What is the mean of this beta distribution?
Why is the beta distribution common in Bayesian models?
options: It is a natural prior for unknown probabilities because its support matches [0, 1].
It is the only distribution that can represent uncertainty.
It guarantees a symmetric posterior.
explanations: Correct. Support and conjugacy make beta especially convenient for probability parameters.
Many distributions represent uncertainty.
Posterior symmetry depends on the parameters and data.
quizzes.answerReason: Beta is a practical probability model because it lives exactly where probabilities live.

quizzes.question: What is a common misuse of a beta model?
options: Applying it to variables that can be negative or exceed 1.
Using it for proportions.
Updating it after binary observations.
explanations: Correct. The support constraint is not optional.
That is one of its best use cases.
That is a standard Bayesian workflow.
quizzes.answerReason: A distribution should respect the legal range of the variable it models.

title: Gaussian Distribution in Practice
description: The Gaussian, or normal, distribution is a symmetric bell-shaped model centered at a mean with spread controlled by a variance. It matters because sums of many small effects tend to look approximately Gaussian, and many estimation methods are built around that approximation. It is central in noise models, z-scores, and many optimization objectives. A common pitfall is assuming every real dataset is Gaussian just because the model is mathematically convenient.
code:
mean = 10
std = 2
z = (14 - mean) / std
print(z)

quizzes.question: What is the z-score of 14 under this Gaussian model?
Why is the Gaussian distribution so widely used?
options: Because it often emerges from many small additive effects and is mathematically convenient.
Because all real measurements are exactly Gaussian.
Because it is only useful for binary labels.
explanations: Correct. The central limit intuition and analytical tractability make it broadly useful.
Real data can be skewed, heavy-tailed, or multimodal.
Binary labels are not Gaussian outcomes.
quizzes.answerReason: Its importance comes from approximation quality and mathematical structure, not universal truth.

quizzes.question: What is the main pitfall of relying on Gaussian assumptions?
options: Ignoring skew, outliers, or heavy tails that change inference and risk estimates.
Having a mean and a variance.
Using standardized values such as z-scores.
explanations: Correct. Misspecified tail behavior can seriously distort conclusions.
Mean and variance are ordinary summaries.
Standardization is useful when the model is appropriate.
quizzes.answerReason: Convenience should not replace checking whether the distribution shape is plausible.

title: Normal Distribution
description: The normal distribution is the canonical symmetric continuous distribution used to model noise, measurement error, and standardized variation. In ML and statistics, it often appears as an assumption behind residuals, priors, or latent variables. It matters because many familiar formulas become simple under normality. A common pitfall is focusing on the bell curve shape while forgetting the independence and equal-variance assumptions often bundled with it in practice.
code:
xs = [8, 10, 12]
mean = sum(xs) / len(xs)
variance = sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in xs) / len(xs)
print(mean)
print(round(variance, 2))

quizzes.question: What are the mean and population variance of the sample?
What parameters define a normal distribution?
options: Its mean and variance.
Its maximum and minimum.
Only its median.
explanations: Correct. Location and spread fully determine the normal family.
Extremes do not define the distribution.
The median alone is insufficient.
quizzes.answerReason: A normal model is completely determined by two parameters: center and spread.

quizzes.question: Why can normality assumptions still fail even if a histogram looks roughly bell-shaped?
options: Because dependence, heteroskedasticity, and tail behavior also matter.
Because normal distributions can never approximate real data.
Because a bell-shaped histogram proves the model is perfect.
explanations: Correct. Shape alone does not validate the full modeling assumptions.
Normal approximations can be very useful.
Visual similarity is not complete validation.
quizzes.answerReason: Statistical assumptions are about more than just the rough silhouette of the data.

title: Log-Normal Distribution
description: A variable is log-normal when its logarithm is normally distributed, which makes the original variable positive and often right-skewed. This matters for modeling incomes, file sizes, response times, and multiplicative growth processes. It is often a better fit than a normal model when values cannot be negative and large outliers are plausible. A common pitfall is fitting a normal model directly to heavily skewed positive data without considering a log transform.
code:
values = [1, 10, 100]
logs = [0, 1, 2]
print(sum(logs) / len(logs))
print(min(values) > 0)

quizzes.question: What does the code print about the logged values and positivity?
When is a log-normal model often more appropriate than a normal model?
options: When the data are strictly positive and show multiplicative or right-skewed behavior.
When the data are binary.
When values are equally likely across a fixed interval.
explanations: Correct. Positivity and skew are classic signs of a log-normal process.
That is a Bernoulli-style setting.
That sounds closer to a uniform distribution.
quizzes.answerReason: Log-normal models are designed for positive variables shaped by multiplicative effects.

quizzes.question: What is the main modeling lesson behind a log-normal distribution?
options: Sometimes the transformed variable has a simpler structure than the raw variable.
Any skewed dataset should always be logged without checking context.
Logging data removes all uncertainty.
explanations: Correct. Modeling often becomes easier after the right transformation.
Transformations should be motivated, not automatic.
Transforms change representation, not the existence of uncertainty.
quizzes.answerReason: Good modeling often depends on choosing a representation where assumptions are more credible.

title: Chi-Square and Sample Variance
description: For normally distributed data, the scaled sample variance follows a chi-square distribution. This matters because variance estimation, confidence intervals for spread, and classical hypothesis tests depend on that relationship. It also explains why uncertainty about variance behaves differently from uncertainty about the mean. A common pitfall is applying chi-square variance formulas without checking whether the normal-data assumption is remotely plausible.
code:
n = 6
sample_variance = 4
scaled = (n - 1) * sample_variance
print(scaled)

quizzes.question: What is the scaled variance quantity?
Why does chi-square appear in variance inference?
options: Because sums of squared standardized normal deviations produce chi-square structure.
Because chi-square is the default distribution for all sample statistics.
Because variance is always discrete.
explanations: Correct. The square-and-sum construction is the key link.
Different statistics have different sampling distributions.
Variance is a continuous quantity.
quizzes.answerReason: The role of chi-square comes from squared Gaussian variation, not from a generic testing rule.

quizzes.question: What is the main caveat in chi-square-based variance inference?
options: It is sensitive to departures from the normality assumption.
It cannot be used with sample sizes larger than 30.
It requires the true variance to be known already.
explanations: Correct. Variance procedures can be distorted by heavy tails or skew.
There is no such upper limit.
The point is to learn about the variance, not to assume it first.
quizzes.answerReason: Variance inference is more assumption-sensitive than many people expect.

title: Sums of Discrete Random Variables and Convolution
description: For discrete variables, convolution combines two probability mass functions into the mass function of their sum. This matters for dice, count aggregation, independent event totals, and dynamic programming over discrete states. It is the discrete counterpart of summing continuous variables through integral convolution. A common pitfall is forgetting to combine only outcome pairs that actually add to the target value.

quizzes.question: What is the probability that two fair dice sum to 7?
What is convolution doing in the discrete case?
options: It adds probabilities from all outcome pairs that produce the same total.
It sorts categories from highest probability to lowest.
It turns a discrete variable into a continuous one.
explanations: Correct. You accumulate mass over all combinations that match the desired sum.
Sorting is unrelated.
Convolution does not change the variable type in that way.
quizzes.answerReason: The output distribution of a sum comes from collecting all ways that sum can happen.

quizzes.question: Why does the sum of two fair dice not have a uniform distribution?
options: Because some totals can be formed by more outcome pairs than others.
Because fair dice are not independent.
Because convolution only works for continuous variables.
explanations: Correct. Middle totals have more combinations than edge totals.
Fair dice are usually modeled as independent.
Convolution works in both discrete and continuous settings.
quizzes.answerReason: Structure in combinatorics creates structure in probability.

title: Fourier Transforms and Characteristic Functions
description: A characteristic function is the Fourier transform of a probability distribution. It encodes the full distribution in a form that makes sums, moments, and convergence results easier to analyze. This matters because difficult probability problems often become simpler after transforming them into another domain. A common pitfall is treating the transform as a mysterious trick instead of as an alternative representation of the same uncertainty.
code:
import cmath
values = [-1, 1]
probs = [0.5, 0.5]
t = 3.141592653589793
phi = sum(p * cmath.exp(1j * t * x) for x, p in zip(values, probs))
print(round(phi.real, 1))

quizzes.question: What is the real part of the characteristic function at t = pi for this symmetric two-point distribution?
Why are characteristic functions useful?
options: They turn some probability operations, especially sums of independent variables, into easier algebraic manipulations.
They are only a visualization tool with no analytical value.
They discard information about the original distribution.
explanations: Correct. Products in transform space correspond to sums in the original space.
They are deeply analytical, not just visual.
Under standard conditions, they uniquely determine the distribution.
quizzes.answerReason: Transforms are valuable because they preserve the distribution while making certain operations simpler.

quizzes.question: What is the right mental model for a transform method?
options: It is a change of representation that can simplify the problem without changing the underlying probability law.
It is a way to avoid defining the random variable.
It is only valid for Gaussian distributions.
explanations: Correct. The distribution is the same object viewed through another lens.
The variable and its law still matter.
Characteristic functions are far more general than Gaussian models.
quizzes.answerReason: A transform is best understood as a useful coordinate system for the same mathematical object.

title: Entropy
description: Entropy measures uncertainty in a probability distribution. High entropy means outcomes are spread out and hard to predict; low entropy means one or a few outcomes dominate. This matters in compression, decision trees, language modeling, and uncertainty-aware evaluation. A common pitfall is treating entropy as a synonym for randomness in general rather than as a precise function of a specific probability distribution.
code:
import math
p = [0.25, 0.25, 0.5]
entropy = -sum(x * math.log2(x) for x in p if x > 0)
print(round(entropy, 2))

quizzes.question: What is the entropy of this distribution in bits?
What does higher entropy mean?
options: The distribution is more uncertain and less concentrated on a single outcome.
The model has higher accuracy.
The data are guaranteed to be uniformly distributed.
explanations: Correct. Entropy tracks uncertainty, not correctness.
Accuracy is a task metric, not entropy.
High entropy does not always mean perfectly uniform.
quizzes.answerReason: Entropy is about how spread out the probability mass is.

quizzes.question: Why does entropy matter in ML?
options: It appears in loss functions, impurity measures, and reasoning about uncertainty.
It only matters in file compression.
It replaces the need for evaluation metrics.
explanations: Correct. Cross-entropy and information gain are standard examples.
Compression is only one application.
Entropy complements, not replaces, evaluation.
quizzes.answerReason: Entropy is one of the core ways ML turns uncertainty into a quantitative object.

title: Multivariate Random Variables and Joint Distributions
description: A multivariate random variable describes uncertainty over several quantities at once, and the joint distribution captures both their individual behavior and their dependence. This matters because features, latent variables, and outputs are rarely isolated in real problems. Many concepts such as covariance, independence, and conditional prediction only make sense in a multivariate view. A common pitfall is modeling variables separately and missing the structure in how they move together.

quizzes.question: What is the marginal probability P(X=1)?
What does a joint distribution provide that marginals alone do not?
options: Information about how variables depend on each other.
A guarantee that each variable is Gaussian.
A way to avoid computing probabilities.
explanations: Correct. Dependence structure is lost if you keep only marginals.
Joint distributions can take many forms.
Probabilities are exactly what they describe.
quizzes.answerReason: The main added value of a joint distribution is relational structure.

quizzes.question: Why is multivariate thinking important in ML?
options: Because models usually consume many features and exploit relationships among them.
Because only one feature should be used in a well-designed model.
Because dependence never affects prediction.
explanations: Correct. The signal often lives in interactions and correlations.
Single-feature models are often too weak.
Dependence can be central to prediction.
quizzes.answerReason: Real modeling is usually about structure across variables, not isolated one-dimensional laws.

title: Functions of Random Variables
description: When you apply a function to a random variable, the uncertainty changes shape along with the values. This matters because predictions, losses, transformations, and feature engineering all create new random variables from old ones. Understanding how means, supports, and distributions change under transformation prevents many modeling mistakes. A common pitfall is transforming the value without reconsidering the resulting distribution or interpretation.
code:
xs = [1, 2, 3]
ys = [x ** 2 for x in xs]
print(ys)
print(sum(ys) / len(ys))

quizzes.question: What transformed values and average are printed?
Why do transformations of random variables matter in ML?
options: Because preprocessing, feature engineering, and model outputs often apply functions that change the uncertainty structure.
Because functions never change distributions.
Because transformations only matter in symbolic algebra.
explanations: Correct. Logs, squares, softmax, and thresholds all reshape distributions.
Transformations often change support, skew, and variance.
This is highly practical, not merely symbolic.
quizzes.answerReason: A transformed variable is a new modeling object with its own behavior.

quizzes.question: What is a common pitfall after transforming a variable?
options: Interpreting the transformed output as if it still lived on the original scale and had the same distribution.
Checking how the support changed.
Using the transformation to simplify structure.
explanations: Correct. Interpretation errors are common after logs, exponentials, or thresholding.
That is a good habit.
That is often the purpose of the transformation.
quizzes.answerReason: Transformation is not just arithmetic. It changes the meaning of the variable.

title: Transforming Two Random Variables into New Variables
description: Two random variables can be combined into new variables such as sums, differences, products, or ratios. This matters because many meaningful quantities in science and ML are derived, not primitive: residuals, margins, log-odds, and normalized scores are all transformed variables. Understanding the mapping helps you reason about support and dependence after transformation. A common pitfall is treating the new variables as independent even when they were built from the same originals.
code:
x = [2, 4, 6]
y = [1, 1, 2]
ratios = [a / b for a, b in zip(x, y)]
print(ratios)
print(max(ratios))

quizzes.question: What are the transformed ratios and their maximum?
Why can transformed pairs become difficult to analyze?
options: Because support, dependence, and density shapes can change in non-obvious ways under the mapping.
Because new variables always become uniformly distributed.
Because transformation removes all information from the original variables.
explanations: Correct. Ratios, products, and nonlinear maps can create complicated distributions.
Uniformity is not guaranteed.
Transformations may preserve or reorganize information, not erase it.
quizzes.answerReason: The difficulty is usually in the geometry of the mapping, not in the arithmetic itself.

quizzes.question: What is a practical example of this idea in ML?
options: Turning logits into probabilities or margins into classification decisions.
Sorting filenames alphabetically.
Using a larger monitor for visualization.
explanations: Correct. Many modeling outputs are transformed versions of underlying random quantities.
That has nothing to do with probability transformation.
That changes presentation, not the random variable.
quizzes.answerReason: Many ML quantities of interest are derived variables built from other uncertain quantities.

title: Estimating a Population Mean from the Sample Mean
description: The sample mean is a basic estimator for the population mean. It matters because it is simple, interpretable, and often the first example of how sampling variability affects inference. In practice, the usefulness of the sample mean depends on data quality, variance, and whether the sampling process is representative. A common pitfall is treating one observed sample average as if it were the exact truth rather than an estimate with uncertainty.
code:
sample = [10, 12, 9, 11, 13]
mean = sum(sample) / len(sample)
print(mean)

quizzes.question: What is the sample mean?
Why is the sample mean such an important estimator?
options: It is a simple summary that often targets the population mean directly and has well-studied sampling behavior.
It is always exact once the sample size is greater than 3.
It does not depend on the data distribution at all.
explanations: Correct. Its value comes from both intuition and statistical theory.
Sample averages still vary from sample to sample.
Distribution and variance still matter.
quizzes.answerReason: The sample mean is foundational because it is both practical and theoretically tractable.

quizzes.question: What is the main thing people forget about a sample mean?
options: It is an estimate that changes across samples and therefore comes with uncertainty.
It is calculated by adding and dividing.
It can be larger than zero.
explanations: Correct. Estimation error is the real lesson, not the arithmetic.
That is obvious but not the main statistical point.
That is irrelevant.
quizzes.answerReason: Inference begins when you recognize that the sample mean is random before the data are observed.

title: Confusion Matrix, Accuracy, Precision, and Recall
description: A confusion matrix breaks classification outcomes into true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives. Accuracy measures overall correctness, precision measures correctness among predicted positives, and recall measures how many actual positives were found. These metrics matter because different mistakes have different costs. A common pitfall is reporting accuracy on an imbalanced problem where precision or recall is the real operational concern.
code:
tp, fp, fn, tn = 30, 10, 5, 55
accuracy = (tp + tn) / (tp + fp + fn + tn)
precision = tp / (tp + fp)
recall = tp / (tp + fn)
print(round(accuracy, 2))
print(round(precision, 2))
print(round(recall, 2))

quizzes.question: What are the accuracy, precision, and recall values?
Why can accuracy be misleading?
options: A model can score high accuracy by dominating the majority class while failing the class you care about.
Accuracy is undefined for classification.
Accuracy ignores true negatives and only counts false positives.
explanations: Correct. Class imbalance often makes accuracy look better than the real behavior.
Accuracy is well-defined.
Accuracy includes all four confusion-matrix cells.
quizzes.answerReason: Accuracy compresses all errors into one number, which can hide asymmetric costs.

quizzes.question: When is recall especially important?
options: When missing a true positive is very costly, such as disease screening or fraud detection.
When false positives are the only thing that matters.
When the labels are continuous values.
explanations: Correct. High recall helps catch as many positives as possible.
That points more toward precision concerns.
Recall is a classification metric.
quizzes.answerReason: Metric choice should reflect the cost of the specific failure mode.

title: Precision-Recall Tradeoff and ROC Curves
description: Thresholded classifiers trade off different kinds of errors, which is why precision, recall, and ROC behavior must be studied across thresholds rather than at just one cutoff. ROC curves summarize true positive rate versus false positive rate, while precision-recall views are often more informative under heavy class imbalance. This matters because operating thresholds are product decisions, not just mathematical defaults. A common pitfall is comparing models only by accuracy at one threshold and ignoring ranking quality.
code:
scores = [0.9, 0.8, 0.4, 0.3]
labels = [1, 0, 1, 0]
threshold = 0.5
preds = [int(s >= threshold) for s in scores]
tp = sum(p == 1 and y == 1 for p, y in zip(preds, labels))
fp = sum(p == 1 and y == 0 for p, y in zip(preds, labels))
precision = tp / (tp + fp)
print(precision)

quizzes.question: What precision results from this threshold?
Why do we study metrics across thresholds?
options: Because the same model can behave very differently depending on the decision threshold.
Because thresholds only matter for regression.
Because ROC curves are built from randomized labels.
explanations: Correct. Scores are turned into decisions only after a threshold is chosen.
Thresholds are central in classification.
ROC curves are computed from model scores and true labels.
quizzes.answerReason: A ranking model and an operational decision rule are related but not identical.

quizzes.question: When is a precision-recall view often more informative than ROC?
options: When positives are rare and false positives matter operationally.
When every class is equally common and mistakes have identical cost.
When the model outputs only one hard label with no score.
explanations: Correct. Precision-recall focuses attention on performance in the positive class.
In balanced settings, ROC may already tell a useful story.
Without scores, threshold curves are limited.
quizzes.answerReason: Class imbalance changes which evaluation view is most revealing.

title: Regression Metrics and Polynomial Regression
description: Regression metrics such as MAE, MSE, and RMSE evaluate prediction error on continuous targets, while polynomial regression expands linear models with nonlinear feature terms. This matters because a model can stay linear in parameters while becoming nonlinear in inputs through engineered features. Metric choice also changes which errors matter most. A common pitfall is using a flexible polynomial fit to chase noise and then mistaking lower training error for better generalization.
code:
y_true = [1, 2, 3]
y_pred = [1, 3, 2]
mae = sum(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(y_true, y_pred)) / len(y_true)
mse = sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(y_true, y_pred)) / len(y_true)
print(round(mae, 2))
print(round(mse, 2))

quizzes.question: What are the MAE and MSE values?
What is the practical difference between MAE and MSE?
options: MSE penalizes large errors more strongly because errors are squared.
MAE can only be used with classification labels.
They always rank models identically.
explanations: Correct. Squaring makes outliers count more heavily.
MAE is a standard regression metric.
Different penalties can change model rankings.
quizzes.answerReason: Loss shape influences which mistakes the model and evaluation care about most.

quizzes.question: What is the main risk of polynomial regression?
options: Adding too many polynomial terms can overfit noise and hurt generalization.
It cannot model curved relationships.
It only works when all coefficients are zero.
explanations: Correct. Flexibility improves fit but can inflate variance.
Polynomial terms are specifically used to capture curvature.
That is false.
quizzes.answerReason: Feature expansion increases expressive power, which also increases overfitting risk.

title: Regression Metrics and Elastic Net
description: Elastic Net combines L1 and L2 regularization to balance sparsity and stability in linear regression. It matters when features are many, correlated, or partially redundant. The regularization strength affects both prediction quality and interpretability, so it must be tuned rather than guessed. A common pitfall is reading shrunk coefficients as if they were the same object as unregularized least-squares estimates.
code:
weights = [1.2, 0.1, -0.05]
l1 = sum(abs(w) for w in weights)
l2 = sum(w * w for w in weights)
alpha = 0.5
penalty = alpha * l1 + (1 - alpha) * l2
print(round(penalty, 3))

quizzes.question: What combined regularization penalty is printed?
Why use Elastic Net instead of only Lasso or only Ridge?
options: It blends sparsity from L1 with stability under correlated features from L2.
It guarantees zero error on the training set.
It removes the need for feature scaling.
explanations: Correct. The mixture can behave better than either extreme alone on real data.
Regularization usually increases training error while helping generalization.
Feature scaling still matters in penalized linear models.
quizzes.answerReason: Elastic Net is a compromise designed for realistic feature spaces, especially correlated ones.

quizzes.question: What is the main interpretation pitfall with regularized coefficients?
options: Shrinkage changes coefficient values, so direct causal-style interpretation becomes more delicate.
Regularization makes coefficients impossible to compute.
A zero coefficient always proves the feature has no signal.
explanations: Correct. Penalization changes the estimator, not just the optimization path.
They are computed routinely.
A feature may be redundant or lose out to correlated alternatives.
quizzes.answerReason: Regularized coefficients are tuned predictive objects, not untouched descriptive summaries.

title: Out-of-Fold Predictions
description: Out-of-fold predictions are generated by predicting each training example from a model that was not trained on that example's fold. This matters because they approximate honest training-set predictions and are useful for stacking, calibration, and leakage-resistant validation. They let you create new features or diagnostics without pretending the model had no access to the example. A common pitfall is mixing in-sample predictions with out-of-fold predictions and accidentally reintroducing leakage.
code:
fold_preds = [0.2, 0.8, 0.6, 0.4]
print(sum(fold_preds) / len(fold_preds))

quizzes.question: What is the average out-of-fold prediction?
Why are out-of-fold predictions useful?
options: They give training-set predictions from models that did not train on the corresponding rows.
They are always better than a separate validation set in every respect.
They eliminate the need for cross-validation.
explanations: Correct. That makes them useful for honest meta-features and diagnostics.
They are useful, but not universally superior in every workflow.
They are produced by cross-validation rather than replacing it.
quizzes.answerReason: The value of OOF predictions is that each row is predicted out of sample relative to the model that produced it.

quizzes.question: What is the main leakage risk in stacking pipelines?
options: Using predictions from models that trained on the same rows those predictions are supposed to represent.
Using any cross-validation at all.
Averaging predictions across folds.
explanations: Correct. In-sample predictions can make the meta-model unrealistically optimistic.
Cross-validation is the protection, not the problem.
Averaging is fine when done carefully.
quizzes.answerReason: OOF logic exists specifically to prevent this form of target leakage.

title: Cross-Validation and Grid Search
description: Cross-validation estimates generalization by rotating which subset of the data is held out, and grid search explores hyperparameter choices under that evaluation loop. This matters because many models are sensitive to settings such as regularization strength, depth, or learning rate. Done properly, the method helps you choose settings without hand-tuning to one lucky split. A common pitfall is peeking at the test set during tuning and turning it into another validation set.
code:
scores = [0.81, 0.79, 0.83, 0.80, 0.77]
cv_score = sum(scores) / len(scores)
print(round(cv_score, 3))

quizzes.question: What is the mean cross-validation score?
Why is cross-validation better than trusting one train-validation split?
options: It reduces dependence on a single lucky or unlucky split by averaging over multiple folds.
It guarantees perfect test performance.
It only matters for unsupervised learning.
explanations: Correct. It gives a more stable view of expected performance.
No validation scheme can guarantee perfect future performance.
Cross-validation is common in supervised settings.
